questions.text: What does 'gross pay' mean?
questions.explanation: Gross pay is your total earnings before any deductions like tax or National Insurance.
questions.tip: Always check your gross pay against your contract to make sure you are being paid correctly.

questions.text: What is net pay?
questions.explanation: Net pay is the amount you actually receive after all deductions have been taken.
questions.tip: Base your monthly budget on your net pay not your gross salary.

questions.text: What is income tax used for?
questions.explanation: Income tax funds public services such as the NHS, schools and roads.
questions.tip: Understanding where your tax goes helps you appreciate the system.

questions.text: What is a personal allowance?
questions.explanation: The personal allowance is the amount you can earn before you start paying income tax.
questions.tip: In the 2025/26 tax year the personal allowance is £12,570.

answers.text: The amount you pay in tax each year
The amount you can earn before paying tax

questions.text: What is a pension?
questions.explanation: A pension is a long term savings plan designed to give you an income when you retire.
questions.tip: Start contributing to your pension as early as possible to benefit from compound growth.

questions.text: What is the first step when creating a personal budget?
questions.explanation: Knowing your income and expenses is the foundation of any budget.
questions.tip: Write down everything you spend for one week to get a clear picture of your habits.

answers.text: Calculate your income and list your expenses

questions.text: What does NI stand for on your payslip?
questions.explanation: National Insurance contributions fund state benefits including the NHS and state pension.
questions.tip: Your NI number is unique to you and stays with you for life.

questions.text: What does it mean to save money?
questions.explanation: Saving means setting aside a portion of your income rather than spending it immediately.
questions.tip: Try to save a little each month even if it is a small amount.

answers.text: Setting aside money for the future

questions.text: What is an employer pension contribution?
questions.explanation: Your employer adds money to your pension on top of your own contributions.
questions.tip: Always contribute enough to get the full employer match as it is essentially free money.

answers.text: Money your employer deducts from your salary
Money your employer adds to your pension

questions.text: What is an emergency fund?
questions.explanation: An emergency fund is money set aside to cover unexpected costs like car repairs or job loss.
questions.tip: Aim to save three to six months of expenses in your emergency fund.

answers.text: Savings set aside for unexpected expenses

questions.text: You earn £30,000 a year. How much of your income is within the basic rate tax band?
questions.explanation: After the personal allowance of £12,570 you pay 20% tax on the remaining £17,430.
questions.tip: Use the Gradigo salary simulator to see exactly how much tax you pay.

questions.text: What is the 50/30/20 budgeting rule?
questions.explanation: The rule suggests spending 50% on needs, 30% on wants and saving 20% of your income.
questions.tip: This is a guideline not a strict rule — adjust it to suit your own situation.

questions.text: Why does starting your pension early matter?
questions.explanation: The earlier you start the more time compound interest has to grow your pension pot.
questions.tip: Even contributing a small amount in your twenties can make a huge difference by retirement.

answers.text: Your money has more time to grow through compound interest

questions.text: What happens if you overspend your budget each month?
questions.explanation: Consistently spending more than you earn leads to debt and financial stress.
questions.tip: Review your spending categories and identify where you can make small cuts.

questions.text: What is compound interest?
questions.explanation: Compound interest means you earn interest on both your original savings and the interest already earned.
questions.tip: The longer you leave money saved the more powerful compound interest becomes.

answers.text: Interest only on your original deposit
Interest earned on both savings and previously earned interest
A fixed monthly payment from your bank

questions.text: What is a tax code and why does it matter?
questions.explanation: A tax code tells your employer how much tax to deduct from your salary each month.
questions.tip: If your tax code is wrong you could be overpaying or underpaying tax so always check it.

answers.text: A code that increases your salary
A code that determines how much tax is deducted from your pay
A code that unlocks pension benefits

questions.text: What is automatic enrolment?
questions.explanation: Automatic enrolment means eligible workers are automatically enrolled into a workplace pension.
questions.tip: You can opt out but it is usually beneficial to stay enrolled especially if your employer contributes.

answers.text: A scheme where you manually apply for a pension
A scheme where eligible workers are automatically enrolled into a pension

questions.text: What is the difference between a fixed and variable expense?
questions.explanation: Fixed expenses stay the same each month like rent while variable expenses change like food shopping.
questions.tip: Variable expenses are usually easier to reduce when you need to cut back.

answers.text: Fixed expenses change monthly while variable stay the same
Fixed expenses stay the same while variable expenses change each month

questions.text: Why is it important to check your payslip each month?
questions.explanation: Checking your payslip helps you spot errors in tax deductions or payments before they become bigger problems.
questions.tip: Keep a copy of each payslip so you can compare them month to month.

answers.text: To spot errors and understand your deductions

questions.text: What is an ISA?
questions.explanation: An ISA is an Individual Savings Account where you can save or invest money without paying tax on the returns.
questions.tip: In the 2025/26 tax year you can save up to £20,000 in an ISA.

questions.text: You earn £50,000 a year. How much income tax do you pay in total?
questions.explanation: You pay 0% on the first £12,570, 20% on £12,571 to £50,270 which is £7,540, and 40% on the remaining £730 which is £292. Total tax is approximately £7,832.
questions.tip: Use the Gradigo salary simulator to check exact figures for your situation.

questions.text: You contribute 5% of your £2,400 monthly salary to your pension and your employer matches 3%. How much goes into your pension each month?
questions.explanation: 5% of £2,400 is £120 and 3% is £72 so £192 total goes into your pension each month.
questions.tip: Use simple percentage calculations to stay on top of your pension contributions.

questions.text: Your monthly income is £2,000. Fixed costs are £1,200 and variable spending is £700. What percentage of your income is left over?
questions.explanation: £2,000 minus £1,900 leaves £100 which is 5% of your income — a very small financial buffer.
questions.tip: Aim for at least a 10 to 20 percent buffer each month to build financial resilience.

questions.text: You receive a £6,000 bonus on top of your £34,000 salary. How much of the bonus is taxed at the higher rate of 40%?
questions.explanation: The higher rate starts at £50,270. Your salary plus bonus is £40,000 which is still below that threshold so none of the bonus is taxed at 40%.
questions.tip: Being pushed into a higher band only affects the income above the threshold not all of your earnings.

questions.text: You save £200 per month at 4% annual compound interest. Approximately how much will you have after 10 years?
questions.explanation: With compound interest your savings grow faster over time. After 10 years you would have approximately £29,500.
questions.tip: Online compound interest calculators can help you visualise long term savings growth.

questions.text: What is the difference between defined benefit and defined contribution pensions?
questions.explanation: A defined benefit pension pays a set income in retirement based on salary and years worked. A defined contribution pension depends on how much was contributed and investment performance.
questions.tip: Most modern workplace pensions are defined contribution so your retirement income depends on your contributions.

answers.text: Defined benefit guarantees an income while defined contribution depends on contributions and investments

questions.text: Your payslip shows a student loan deduction. You are on Plan 2. At what income threshold do repayments start?
questions.explanation: Plan 2 student loan repayments begin when you earn over £28,470 per year in the 2025/26 tax year.
questions.tip: Repayments are automatically deducted through PAYE so you do not need to do anything manually.

questions.text: What is the lifetime allowance for pension savings?
questions.explanation: The lifetime allowance was abolished in April 2024 meaning there is no longer a limit on how much you can save in a pension without a tax charge.
questions.tip: Always check current HMRC guidance as pension rules can change.

questions.text: You have £5,000 in savings earning 2% interest and £3,000 in credit card debt at 20% interest. What is the most financially smart move?
questions.explanation: The interest you pay on the debt is much higher than what you earn on savings so paying off the debt first saves more money overall.
questions.tip: High interest debt almost always costs more than savings earn so prioritise paying it off.

answers.text: Keep saving and ignore the debt
Pay off the high interest debt first
Split your savings equally between debt and savings

questions.text: What does it mean to be in a higher tax band?
questions.explanation: Only the income above the threshold for the higher band is taxed at the higher rate. Your income below the threshold is still taxed at lower rates.
questions.tip: Earning more is always beneficial even if it pushes you into a higher tax band.

answers.text: All of your income is taxed at the higher rate
Only income above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate
You stop receiving a personal allowance
